results.name: Time to fluency (SM84): in the stage 2 simulator of response-time prediction (SM82), how many reviews and seconds until a card is first answered Good in under 3.9 s, by desired retention and interval-growth policy
results.eval: 150 users of the 732 set; simulator with each user’s FSRS-6 parameters and the answer-time head’s cost and speed curves (cost model C)
results.fork: Fluent = first Good under 3.9 s
results.takeaway: Fluency is mostly about the user, and higher retention makes it cheaper: at desired retention 0.90, 37.5% of cards are fluent by day 365 (4.9 reviews, 99 s each; 312 s per fluent card counting the cards that never get there); 67% for the fastest third of users vs 17% for the slowest. results.name: Session position effect on answer time (SM85): is the speed-up later in the day’s reviews warm-up or which cards come late? Card and day fixed effects plus controls

results.fork: vs the first 10 reviews of the day
results.takeaway: Mostly real, not just card order: the same card is answered 27.6% faster [23.7, 31.6] at reviews 201–400 of the day and 34% faster [29.8, 37.9] from the 401st on, with fast Goods +6.2 / +9.3 points; monotone, seen in 95% of users with 5,000+ reviews. Selection explains ~40–45% of the raw gap (mostly which users do long days). It follows the number of reviews done, not minutes. A free reorder (slowest cards late) would save ~55 s a day [48, 63] (~4% of review time): an upper bound. User’s reading (11-01): most likely rushing late in long sessions, so no reordering is planned

detail.verdict: Measurement: within-card speed-up with position in the day; warm-up and rushing late cannot be told apart (Again share only 0.123 → 0.139)
notes: Controls: elapsed days, the card’s review count, lapses, previous time and grade, predicted recall. With users weighted equally: −26.6% at 201–400. results.fork: Within-user differences in lapses (first 10 reviews), leech share and reviews spent
results.takeaway: The prize is large, the levers found so far are small: the worst 5% of cards take 16.6% of all reviews, the worst 10% take 27.2%. Cards from 2–9-card notes lapse about 6–7% less than single-card notes (−0.025 per card in the first 10 reviews); 10+ cards no gain. A sibling seen earlier the same day mostly tells the note’s difficulty (a failed sibling: −11 to −13 points pass rate), not a memory boost; no lasting effect. All correlational

detail.verdict: Nothing to change in scheduling yet; next are the natural experiments (interval fuzz, missed days) and early spacing, then the early won’t-stick flag
